{{Short description|On lattices and sphere packing in Euclidean space}}
'''Hilbert's eighteenth problem''' is [[Hilbert problems|one of the 23 problems]] set out in a celebrated list compiled in 1900 by mathematician [[David Hilbert]]. It asks three separate questions on the space group in <math> n </math>-dimensional [[Euclidean space]], [[anisohedral tiling]] in three-dimensional Euclidean space, and the densest sphere packing in [[Kepler conjecture]].{{r|milnor}} Respectively, these questions were answered affirmatively by [[Ludwig Bieberbach]], [[Karl Reinhardt (mathematician)|Karl Reinhardt]], and [[Thomas Callister Hales]].

== First question: symmetry groups in {{math|1=''n''}} dimensions==
{{further information|Space group#Bieberbach's theorems}}
The first question in Hilbert's problem asks whether there are only finitely many essentially different [[space group]]s in <math>n</math>-dimensional [[Euclidean space]]. Here, a space group or crystallographic group is the [[symmetry group]] of a repeating pattern in space, usually in three dimensions, with its [[symmetry operation]] as the [[rigid transformation]]s of the pattern that leave it unchanged.{{r|senechal}}

This question was answered affirmatively by [[Ludwig Bieberbach]].{{r|senechal}} Named as Bieberbach group, Bieberbach proved that the subgroup of translations of any such group contains <math> n </math> linearly independent translations, and is a [[Free abelian group|free abelian]] subgroup of finite index, and is also the unique maximal normal abelian subgroup. Bieberbach also showed that, in any dimension <math> n </math>, there are only a finite number of possibilities for the [[Isomorphism theorems|isomorphism]] class of the underlying group of a space group, and the action of the group on Euclidean space is moreover unique up to [[Conjugation of isometries in Euclidean space|conjugation]] by [[affine transformation]]s.{{r|bieberbach}}

== Second question: anisohedral tiling in three dimensions ==
{{further|Anisohedral tiling}}
{{multiple image
| image1            = Karl Reinhardt's polyhedron.svg
| caption1          = Two views of the three-dimensional polyhedron (one lying flat, the other on the side) as interpreted from Reinhardt's 1928 booklet
| image2            = Heesch anisohedral tiling.svg
| caption2          = Two-dimensional plane by Heesch's anisohedral partial tile
| total_width       = 400
}}
The second question in Hilbert's problem asks whether there exists a [[polyhedron]] in [[Three-dimensional space|three-dimensional Euclidean space]] that [[tessellation of space|tiles]] but not the [[fundamental region]] of any space group. In other words, the second problem asked which tiles, but does not admit an [[Isohedral figure|isohedral]] (tile-[[Group action (mathematics)|transitive]]) tiling. Such tiles are not equivalent under any symmetry of the tiling, which are now known as [[anisohedral tiling|anisohedral]]. Posing the problem in three dimensions, Hilbert probably assumed that no such tile exists in two dimensions; this assumption later proved to be incorrect.{{r|gs}}

Such a three dimensions polyhedron was found by [[Karl Reinhardt (mathematician)|Karl Reinhardt]] in his 1928 booklet titled ''Zur Zerlegung der euklidischen Räume in kongruente Polytope''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Reinhardt |first=Karl |url=https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Zur_Zerlegung_der_euklidischen_R%C3%A4ume_in_kongruente_Polytope_Reinhardt_1928.pdf |title=Zur Zerlegung der euklidischen Räume in kongruente Polytope |publisher=Sitzungsberichte der Preussischen Akamemie der Wissenschaften Berlin, Physikalisch-Mathematische Klasse |publication-date=1928 |page=150–155 |trans-title=On the decomposition of Euclidean spaces into congruent polytopes}}</ref> The first example in two dimensions was found by [[Heinrich Heesch]] in 1935.{{r|heesch|edwards}}

The [[einstein problem]], where "einstein" means "one stone" in German's [[word play]], is the natural extension of Hilbert's eighteenth problem's second question. The problem asks for a shape that can tile space but not with an [[infinite cyclic group]] of symmetries.{{r|goodman}} Equivalently, it asks the existence of a single [[prototile]] that forms an [[aperiodic set of prototiles|aperiodic set]], a shape that can tessellate space but only in a non-periodic way.{{r|senechal}} It was solved in 2024 by [[David Smith (amateur mathematician)|David Smith]] and his colleagues.{{r|smkg}}

== Third question: densest sphere packing ==
{{main|Kepler conjecture}}

The third question in Hilbert's problem asks for the densest [[sphere packing]] or packing of other specified shapes. Although it expressly includes shapes other than spheres, it is generally taken as equivalent to the [[Kepler conjecture]]. The conjecture was named after 17th-century German mathematician [[Johannes Kepler]] in his booklet titled ''Strena, seu, de Nieu Sexangula''. It states that the packing of equal volume spheres has a density greater than the packing of the [[face-centered cubic]] arrangement. Such a density is{{r|lagarias}}
<math display="block"> \frac{\pi}{3\sqrt{2}} = 0.74048.</math>

In 1998, American mathematician [[Thomas Callister Hales]] gave a [[computer-aided proof]] of the Kepler conjecture. It shows that the most space-efficient way to pack spheres is in a pyramid shape.{{r|hales}}
